notes:
I've written notes on all 19 verses below. Three limits first:

- **Catholic, Orthodox and modern scholarship sites:** I found nothing on Leviticus 5 from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org. The only Catholic item is a Douay-Rheims translation difference at v. 5, and a few modern scholars come up only where older commentaries mention them.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith and hyper-grace teaching:** none of the pages I read mentioned these, so they are left out.
- **Differences between Protestant traditions:** the pages I read show no real denominational split on this chapter. The disagreements are between individual commentators, mainly over whether vv. 1–13 describe the sin offering or the guilt offering, and over the bloodless offering in v. 11. Where I name a commentator's tradition, that label is my own and not taken from the page.

---

**Chapter overview**
- The question running through the chapter is how the two offerings differ. Matthew Henry says the difference lay not so much in the sacrifices themselves, and the management of them, as in the occasions of the offering of them. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_005.cfm
- Precept Austin's chart calls vv. 4:1–5:13 the sin offering, picturing Christ as "Substitute". It calls vv. 5:14–6:7 the guilt offering, picturing Christ's "Satisfaction" of God's demands. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_5_commentary
- Constable says the Hebrew word *'asham*, translated "guilt," also means "reparation." He suggests calling it a reparation or compensation offering, because other sacrifices also deal with guilt. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/leviticus-5.html

**v. 1: Failing to testify**
- **Traditional reading (Ellicott).** When a court could not prove a case, the judge would solemnly call on anyone with knowledge to come forward. Someone who knew but stayed silent was considered in the sight of God as participating in the transgression which he had thus concealed. Ellicott links this to Proverbs 29:24 and to the high priest putting Jesus under oath in Matthew 26:63. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
- **Deliberate or accidental?** Ellicott says that, unlike the accidental sins of chapter 4, this is designed and culpable silence, and of deliberately concealing a crime. — same URL
- **Guzik (Enduring Word).** Not telling lies wasn't enough; God also required His people to make the truth known. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-5/
- **Matthew Henry.** Jewish judges could put even the suspect under oath, which is why Jesus answered once the high priest adjured him. Henry urges anyone called as a witness to give full, open evidence. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
- **Modern scholarship, as reported by Coffman.** Martin Noth read the verse as being about someone who hears another person curse publicly, and Ronald Clements agreed. Coffman sides with Keil, who said the word means a judicial oath, not cursing in general. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html

**vv. 2–3: Touching uncleanness**
- **Guzik.** This was *ceremonial* guilt, not moral guilt. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-5/
- **Ellicott.** Touching a carcass normally made someone unclean only until evening, and washing removed it. The offering was needed only when carelessness made the person forget to wash and he later remembered. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** The touch itself was only ceremonial. But his neglect to wash himself according to the law was such an instance either of carelessness or contempt as contracted a moral guilt. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
- **Coffman's example.** Someone could stumble onto an unmarked grave by accident. He links this to the whitewashed tombs of Jesus' day (Matthew 23:27). — same URL
- **Text note (Ellicott).** The Greek Septuagint leaves out the end of v. 2, which also repeats the wording of v. 3. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm

**v. 4: Rash oaths**
- **Ellicott.** The verse covers an oath made in thoughtlessness or in passion. "Good or evil" is a figure of speech meaning any action at all. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
- **Guzik.** A careless promise was still a promise before the LORD and had to be observed. If the promise was not kept it had to be atoned for by a sin offering. He adds that such vows may be the legitimate, decisive expression of a move of the Holy Spirit in a person's life, but a broken vow must be confessed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-5/
- **Matthew Henry's dilemma.** A person is guilty if he do not perform his oath, and yet, if the matter of it were evil, guilty if he do. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_005.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary (J.A. Macdonald).** The lesson is to be slow to swear. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-5.html

**v. 5: Confession**
- **Gill (Baptist).** The confession had to name the particular sin, not sin in general. Without it the offering was worthless. He reports a Jewish tradition that the offerer confessed while laying his hand on the animal. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/5-5.htm
- **Guzik.** Confessing means agreeing with God that the sin was wrong. Without confession the sacrifice "would do no good," otherwise it would amount to treating the ritual like magic. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-5/
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist).** Paying back what was owed was not enough without confession, because the confession of sin has a direct tendency to humble the soul. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-5.html
- **Bonar (via Precept Austin).** This is the first explicit command to confess, because these sins were "hidden." Precept Austin connects it to 1 John 1:9. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_5_commentary
- **Catholic translation.** The Douay-Rheims renders this verse Let him do penance for his sin. That is a translation note only; I found no Catholic commentary on the verse. — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/5-5.htm

**v. 6: Female lamb or goat**
- **Which offering is this?** Commentators disagree.
  - Barnes, Keil (via Coffman), Kelly and Pulpit say *'asham* here means "his guilt" or "his forfeit," not the separate guilt offering that begins at v. 14. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
  - Ellicott says the opposite: "trespass offering" is the right rendering, and vv. 1–13 describe that offering. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
  - Gill says it is hard to state the difference, since the same offering is here called both a trespass offering and a sin offering. He sees it as a type of Christ, whose soul was made an *'asham* in Isaiah 53:10. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
- **Why a female animal (Poole)?** These sins were committed unknowingly and were lesser, so God accepted a meaner sacrifice for them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/5-6.htm
- **No ranking by status (Ellicott).** Unlike chapter 4, no distinction is made by rank here; priest, ruler and layman bring the same animal. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm

**vv. 7–10: Two birds for the poor**
- **Why two birds (Ellicott, Bridgeway)?** One bird can't be divided into the altar portion and the rest, so one is offered as the sin offering and the other burned whole. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
- **Guzik.** The sin offering always came first, then the burnt offering, which pictured renewed commitment and consecration. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-5.cfm
- **v. 8 (Ellicott).** The head is not fully severed, unlike the bird burnt offering in Leviticus 1:15. He also describes how priests did this in the Second Temple period. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
- **v. 9 (Ellicott).** The blood is simply splashed on the altar wall. In the regular sin offering it was also put on the altar's horns. — same URL
- **Barnes.** The second bird, as a burnt offering, stood for the worshipper's dedication. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
- **Bible Hub.** Mary and Joseph's offering of birds in Luke 2:24 echoes this provision. — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/5.htm

**vv. 11–13: Flour for the very poorest**
- **Matthew Henry.** no man's poverty shall ever be a bar in the way of his pardon. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_005.cfm
- **No oil or frankincense.**
  - Ellicott: adding them would make it a grain offering, not a sin offering. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
  - Matthew Henry: leaving them out shows how loathsome sin is. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-11.html
  - Guzik, quoting another writer: oil and frankincense signal joy, so they are left out. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-5.cfm
- **How can a bloodless offering atone? (the point most debated here)**
  - Guzik (Enduring Word): God looked to the heart and not the nature of the sacrifice itself. — same URL
  - Kelly: the flour is the exception which proves the rule, a substitute allowed because of poverty. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-11.html
  - Bridgeway: the flour was placed on the altar with the blood of the other offerings, so atonement still rested on blood. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
  - Ligonier (Reformed): the grain offerings worked only because of the yearly blood sacrifice of the Day of Atonement (Lev 16). This answers the apparent conflict with Hebrews 9:22. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/without-blood
  - Calvin (Reformed): the poor man's flour reconciled him to God as fully as the rich man's animal. This shows God's aim was to point everyone to the one Mediator, and Calvin rejects the pagan idea that a pure heart alone pleases God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-6.html
- **v. 12 (Ellicott).** A handful is burned as a memorial; the priest eats the rest. If a priest was the offender, all of the flour was burned. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm

**v. 14: A new section**
- **Ellicott.** The opening formula shows this was a separate message to Moses. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/5.htm
- **Coffman.** The guilt offering proper begins here, not in v. 6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-5.html

**v. 15: Sins against holy things**
- **Matthew Henry.** Examples: unknowingly using tithes, firstfruits or firstborn animals for oneself, or eating the priests' portions (Lev 22:14–16). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_005.cfm
- **Coffman.** Mostly sins of omission, such as carelessly failing to pay tithes. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/leviticus-5.html
- **"Of proper value in silver."** Some take this to allow paying money instead of a ram; others say it is just the ram's value. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_5_commentary
- **Milgrom (via Precept Austin).** The sin offering covers "any of the commandments," while the guilt offering is specifically about consecrated "holy things." — same URL

**v. 16: Restitution plus a fifth**
- **Guzik.** When holy things had been desecrated in some way, a mere sin offering was not enough. The person repaid the loss plus 20%. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-5/
- **Gill.** The added fifth shows how serious sacrilege is, even when done unknowingly. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-16.html
- **Wiersbe (via Precept Austin).** True repentance will always bring with it a desire for restitution. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_5_commentary
- **Jamieson, quoted by Coffman.** The main idea is not expiation, but compensation, or restitution of a debt due to Jehovah as King of Israel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-16.html
- **Calvin.** He calls it "gross ignorance" to treat this offense as greater than the sins of vv. 1–13. The passage simply tells how a thoughtless person gets pardon for not fully paying his vows or offerings. — same URL

**vv. 17–19: Sin without knowing it**
- **Guzik.** "I didn't know" was no excuse. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-5/ He also notes that Sins of ignorance do differ from sins done with knowledge in the degree of guilt. Enduring Word credits this insight to Spurgeon (Baptist). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-5.cfm
- **Matthew Henry.** These verses cover cases where a person only suspected he had sinned. He brought the offering and repaid the value, but did not add the fifth. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_005.cfm
- **Constable.** The person brought the offering when he became aware of his sin or even suspected his guilt. Constable adds that repentance reduced the guilt to that of an accidental act. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/leviticus-5.html
- **Deffinbaugh (bible.org).** He uses Joshua's treaty with the Gibeonites as an example of guilt incurred unknowingly. He sees the offering as grace for Israelites who felt they fell short "yet not knowing why." — https://bible.org/seriespage/6-guilt-offering-leviticus-514-67-71-6
- **Gill on v. 19.** No sin, however committed, is forgiven without atonement by sacrifice. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/5-19.html
- **Fulfillment in Christ.** Guzik connects the guilt offering to Isaiah 53:10 and Romans 4:25 as fulfilled in Christ. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
